title: The Tyranny of the Optimised Life
focus: Inversion and 'were it not for' conditionals
paragraphs: Daniela, a friend of mine who works in logistics in Bogotá, recently showed me her phone with something close to pride. It tracked her sleep, her steps, her monthly spending in pesos, the pages she read each week and even the minutes she had spent talking to her mother. Nowhere in the dashboard, however, was there a column for enjoyment. When I pointed this out, she laughed and replied that enjoyment was rather hard to quantify. That, I suspect, is precisely the trouble, and it is the subject of this essay.

We are living through a quiet conversion of leisure into project. A walk must reach ten thousand steps to count; a book must be finished to be worth having started; a friendship is 'maintained' like a piece of machinery. Seldom do we ask who set these targets, or why they are so tidy. Were it not for the apps, I doubt that most of us would ever have invented them, and yet we now treat them as though they were laws of nature rather than the decisions of a few designers who wished us to keep tapping.

Defenders of the optimised life argue, not unreasonably, that measurement brings honesty. Memory flatters us; numbers do not. A person who believes she sleeps seven hours and discovers that she sleeps five has been given something valuable. I concede the point without reservation. What I resist is the leap from information to obligation, from 'this is what happened' to 'this is what you must now improve'. The first is knowledge; the second is a quiet form of management, and we have appointed ourselves as our own harshest managers.

There is a historical irony here that deserves a mention. The ideal of the efficient worker, once imposed by factory owners armed with a stopwatch, has been so thoroughly adopted by individuals that no supervisor is needed any longer. We have outsourced the foreman to our own pockets. The stopwatch has not disappeared; it has merely learned to congratulate us. Rarely has a system of control been so cheaply maintained, and never, perhaps, has it been so warmly welcomed by the very people it controls.

None of this means that planning is foolish or that ambition is a disease. A student preparing for a scholarship interview in Lima has good reason to organise her weeks, and nobody should sneer at her calendar. The distinction I wish to draw is between a tool that serves a purpose and a habit that has quietly become the purpose. Once the tracking outlasts the goal, we are no longer improving our lives; we are merely auditing them, and an audit, however thorough, has never made anybody happy.

Consider what is lost when everything is counted. The afternoon spent doing nothing in particular, the conversation that wandered for two hours and produced no decision, the film watched only because the rain would not stop: such moments leave no data and, in the logic of the dashboard, no value. Yet ask anyone to describe the happiest day of the past year, and I would wager that very few would choose the one with the best score. Some things resist measurement precisely because they matter.

Daniela, to her credit, took my argument with good humour. Last week she sent me a message: she had switched off every notification for a fortnight and could not tell me how many steps she had walked. She could tell me, however, that she had spent a whole Sunday afternoon talking to her mother, with nobody keeping time. 'It was unquantifiable,' she wrote. 'I recommend it.' I could not have put the case better myself, and I did not try.
glossary: panel de control con datos y gráficos
halagar, favorecer de forma poco realista

questions.q: Daniela's phone recorded the time she spent talking to her mother.
questions.explain_es: El texto dice que registraba 'even the minutes she had spent talking to her mother'.

questions.q: The author claims that measuring one's habits is always dishonest.
questions.explain_es: Al contrario: admite que la medición aporta honestidad ('I concede the point without reservation') y que los números no halagan.

questions.q: What can we infer from Daniela's final message?
options: She found the unmeasured afternoon more satisfying than her data
She intends to persuade her mother to try the same app
She regrets having abandoned her tracking for a fortnight
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: llama 'unquantifiable' a la tarde sin medir y escribe 'I recommend it'; solo la primera opción es coherente con ese entusiasmo. No expresa arrepentimiento ni habla de su madre usando la aplicación.

questions.q: How does the author treat Daniela throughout the essay?
options: With cool and purely scientific detachment
With open contempt for her choices
With affectionate, good-humoured irony
questions.explain_es: Tono: habla de ella con simpatía ('to her credit', 'good humour') y bromea con suavidad, sin desprecio ni frialdad.

questions.q: Why does the author mention the student preparing for a scholarship interview?
options: To suggest that students plan their weeks too little
To show that scholarships require careful tracking apps
To clarify that planning itself is not his target
questions.explain_es: Propósito: matiza que organizar el tiempo no es el problema ('nobody should sneer at her calendar'); critica el hábito que se vuelve el fin.

questions.q: What does the author do in the third paragraph?
options: He cites a study to support his thesis
He grants a point before limiting its reach
He rejects an argument and later accepts it
questions.explain_es: Estructura: concede que medir da honestidad y luego marca el límite: 'What I resist is the leap from information to obligation'.

questions.q: In 'nobody should sneer at her calendar', 'sneer' means…
options: add something to it quickly
speak about it with scorn
look at it with great care
questions.explain_es: 'Sneer at' es burlarse con desprecio. El autor dice que nadie debería hacerlo, pues planificar tiene sentido para ella.

title: Review: The Salt Archive, a Novel That Mistakes Silence for Depth
paragraphs: It is a rare novel that announces its ambitions on the first page and then spends three hundred more politely declining to fulfil them. The Salt Archive, the second book by the Peruvian writer Mariana Quispe, opens with an archivist named Elías discovering a box of undated letters in a municipal basement. Within a paragraph we sense that something important lies buried there. Within a chapter we realise, with a certain weariness, that it will stay buried.

Let me be fair at once: Quispe is a gifted stylist. Her sentences have a dry, mineral clarity, and she can describe a damp stairwell or the smell of old paper so precisely that the reader begins to cough. If prose alone made a novel, this would be a masterpiece. Unfortunately, novels also require something to happen, and here the author seems to regard events as a form of vulgarity, rather like raising one's voice at a funeral.

The letters, we are told, were written by a woman whose name Elías cannot read. He photographs them, files them, loses sleep over them and, in the book's most dramatic scene, moves them to a higher shelf. Quispe clearly intends this restraint as a statement about how history reaches us: in fragments, mostly illegible, and always a little late. It is an interesting idea. It would be a more interesting idea were it not repeated, with minor variations, in every chapter.

Elías himself is the novel's quiet casualty. He is described as 'a man who listened to rooms', a phrase that is lovely the first time and faintly alarming the fourth. He has no appetite, no debts, no friends worth naming and no opinions about the city's unpaid salaries, though his office is plainly short of money. One begins to suspect that the character has been emptied on purpose, to leave space for the reader. Alas, the reader is left with nothing but space.

Admirers will say that I am demanding a plot from a book that never promised one, and the objection has some force. Not every novel needs to resolve its mystery; some of the best leave a door open on purpose. But there is a difference between an open door and a blank wall with a handle painted on it. The final pages gesture towards a revelation, then withdraw it with such elaborate politeness that one almost apologises for having asked.

There are, to be sure, pleasures along the way. A subplot about the archive's cat, who sleeps on the only warm radiator, is the funniest thing in the book and also the most alive. A brief chapter in which Elías visits his sister's bakery crackles with the energy the rest of the novel suppresses. One wishes Quispe had trusted these moments, and trusted herself enough to let her narrator want something badly, even something small.

I closed the book with respect and no excitement, which is a curious combination for a reviewer to report. Quispe will undoubtedly write a major novel; the evidence is on every page, in the sentences themselves. The Salt Archive is not that novel. It is an elegant rehearsal for it, and like most rehearsals, it is admirable chiefly to those who already know how the performance will go.
glossary: escritor con un estilo cuidado y personal

questions.q: The reviewer admires the quality of Quispe's sentences.
questions.explain_es: Dice que Quispe 'is a gifted stylist' y que sus frases tienen 'a dry, mineral clarity'.

questions.q: According to the reviewer, the novel's most dramatic scene involves a violent argument.
questions.explain_es: Ironía: la escena 'más dramática' consiste en que Elías mueve las cartas 'to a higher shelf'. No hay discusión violenta.

questions.q: What does the reviewer imply about Quispe's next book?
options: It will repeat the same mistakes again
It will probably be better than this one
It will be published without any plot
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: 'Quispe will undoubtedly write a major novel' y 'The Salt Archive is... an elegant rehearsal for it' indican que esperan algo mejor.

questions.q: What is the tone of the phrase 'the reader is left with nothing but space'?
options: Wry criticism of an empty narrative
Neutral description of the book's setting
Sincere praise for the novel's openness
questions.explain_es: Tono: es una ironía. Retoma 'to leave space for the reader' para decir que el personaje vacío no deja nada más que vacío.

questions.q: Why does the reviewer mention the archive's cat and the bakery chapter?
options: To prove that the novel has a clear plot
To argue that Quispe writes only about animals
To show moments where the book comes alive
questions.explain_es: Propósito: son lo 'most alive' y lo que 'crackles with energy'; sirven de contraste con el resto, que el reseñista considera contenido en exceso.

questions.q: How is the review organised?
options: Plot summary only, followed by a list of awards won
Praise first, then growing reservations, then a balanced verdict
Personal memories of the author followed by an interview
questions.explain_es: Estructura: empieza con elogio del estilo, acumula reservas (trama, personaje, final) y termina con un veredicto matizado: respeto, pero sin entusiasmo.

questions.q: In 'a blank wall with a handle painted on it', the image suggests something…
options: protective
decorative
deceptive
questions.explain_es: La imagen de una puerta pintada en una pared evoca algo engañoso: promete una apertura (revelación) que no existe.

title: The Honest Placebo
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, the placebo was medicine's awkward relative: useful as a control in experiments, embarrassing in the consulting room. A placebo, after all, is a treatment with no active ingredient, and its effect was long assumed to depend on deception. If a patient knew that the pill was sugar, the reasoning went, the benefit would evaporate. A series of small but provocative experiments has since suggested that this assumption may be wrong, or at least too simple.

The most discussed of these was a trial published in 2010 involving patients with irritable bowel syndrome, a painful and stubborn condition. One group received no treatment. Another received pills described, quite openly, as inert and made of sugar, though the participants were told that such pills had produced improvement in other people through mind-body processes. After a few weeks, the second group reported significantly greater relief. The trial was small, and the authors themselves urged caution, but the result was difficult to ignore.

How could such a thing work? Researchers propose several mechanisms, none of which is magical. Expectation changes how the brain processes pain and nausea; the ritual of taking a pill, and the attention of a clinician, may reduce stress; and learned associations, built up over a lifetime of effective medicines, may prime the body to respond. What the placebo does not do is shrink a tumour or cure an infection. Its domain is largely subjective symptoms, those that depend on how the patient experiences them.

This limitation matters, because popular accounts have a tendency to inflate the placebo into a kind of universal remedy. It is not. Nor does an improvement in reported pain prove that the underlying disease has changed. A patient may feel better and be no better, and a good clinician must distinguish between the two. The honest placebo, in other words, is not an alternative to medicine but a reminder that the experience of illness is partly shaped by context.

The ethical implications are more intriguing than the clinical ones. Traditionally, prescribing a placebo meant lying to a patient, and the medical profession has rightly regarded this as unacceptable. If the effect survives transparency, however, the dilemma changes shape. A doctor could say, truthfully, that a pill contains no active drug and that evidence suggests it may help some people. Such candour would respect the patient's autonomy while still harnessing the surprising power of expectation.

Sceptics offer reasonable objections. Many of the experiments are small, short and dependent on self-reported symptoms, which are notoriously susceptible to influence. Some patients may guess that the researchers hope for improvement and oblige them. Larger studies, with more rigorous designs, are required before any clinical guidelines could responsibly be changed. Enthusiasm, in this field as in any other, should be proportionate to the quality of the evidence.

What is already clear is that the old picture, in which a placebo is simply a trick, no longer holds. The mind is not an inert spectator of treatment; it takes part in it. Whether that participation can be used deliberately, safely and without deception remains an open question. It is, at least, a question worth asking honestly, which is more than the history of the placebo can usually claim.
glossary: grupo o condición de control en un experimento

questions.q: In the 2010 trial, participants in one group knew that their pills contained no active drug.
questions.explain_es: Las píldoras estaban descritas 'quite openly, as inert and made of sugar'.

questions.q: The article says that placebos can shrink tumours.
questions.explain_es: El texto afirma lo contrario: 'What the placebo does not do is shrink a tumour or cure an infection'.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the author's view of the 2010 trial?
options: It was interesting but too limited to be decisive
It was conclusive and should change guidelines
It was flawed and should have been ignored
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: es 'small' y los autores 'urged caution', pero 'difficult to ignore'. Se pide más investigación antes de cambiar guías clínicas.

questions.q: What is the author's attitude towards popular accounts of the placebo?
options: Enthusiastic and uncritical
Totally dismissive of all of them
Mildly critical of their exaggeration
questions.explain_es: Actitud: señala que tienden 'to inflate the placebo into a kind of universal remedy', es decir, una crítica moderada y no un rechazo total.

questions.q: Why does the author discuss the ethical implications?
options: To prove that doctors have always lied to patients
To show that open placebos might remove a traditional dilemma
To argue that placebos should replace medicines
questions.explain_es: Propósito: si el efecto sobrevive a la transparencia, 'the dilemma changes shape': el médico puede ser sincero y aun así beneficiarse de la expectativa.

questions.q: How does the article move from the fourth paragraph to the sixth?
options: From explanation to implication to objections
From a joke to a statistic to a conclusion
From a case study to a personal story
questions.explain_es: Estructura: los límites y la ética (implicaciones) preceden a las objeciones de los escépticos; el artículo se mueve de explicar a considerar consecuencias y críticas.

questions.q: In 'self-reported symptoms, which are notoriously susceptible to influence', 'susceptible to' means…
options: carefully protected from
easily affected by
rarely noticed during
questions.explain_es: 'Susceptible to' significa 'fácilmente influenciable por': los síntomas declarados pueden verse afectados por lo que el paciente cree que se espera.

title: Libraries Are Not a Luxury
paragraphs: When a city council needs to save money, it tends to begin with whatever cannot protest. Parks lose their gardeners, street lamps are dimmed, and libraries are quietly asked to close two hours earlier. The latest proposal in Guadalajara, which would shorten opening hours at several neighbourhood libraries in order to save a modest sum, is presented as a technicality. It is nothing of the kind. It is a statement about what the city thinks reading is for.

Consider who actually uses a library after six in the evening. Not the people who own shelves of books and fast internet, but the nursing assistant finishing a shift, the teenager whose flat has one table shared by four people, the retired man who comes for the newspapers and the company. For them, the evening hours are not an extra; they are the only hours available. Cutting them does not reduce a service. It removes it from precisely those who have nowhere else to turn.

The council argues, with some justice, that budgets are finite and that every peso spent on one thing is a peso withheld from another. We do not dispute this. Nor do we pretend that libraries are the only deserving cause in a city with potholes, overcrowded buses and a hospital waiting list. But a budget is also a moral document. How can a city that hosts one of the world's great book fairs justify turning off the lights on its own readers?

There is a further, quieter cost. A library is one of the few public places where nobody is asked to buy anything. One may sit for three hours without ordering a coffee, learn to use a computer without paying a fee, or simply be warm. In an age when almost every room we enter expects a transaction, such places are not merely useful but rare. Once they are gone, they are not easily rebuilt, because the habit of using them goes with them.

Defenders of the cuts will say that books are available online and that digital access makes buildings unnecessary. This confuses a collection with an institution. A library is not only a store of texts; it is a room full of other people reading, a librarian who knows what to recommend to a nervous twelve-year-old, a place that teaches by example that attention is something one can share. A download, however convenient, offers none of these.

Nothing here is an argument against reform. If opening hours are poorly matched to demand, they should be adjusted, and the council is entitled to look at usage data. We would welcome a proposal that moved hours towards the evenings and weekends, when working families can actually attend. What we reject is the assumption that saving a small amount justifies a large and lasting loss, and that those who will pay the price are too few, or too quiet, to matter.

We therefore urge the council to withdraw the proposal and to open its books, as it asks the library to open its doors. If a smaller saving is genuinely needed, let it be found where the damage is less visible and less unfair. Cities are judged, in the end, by what they refuse to cut. A place that will not close its libraries tells its citizens that their minds, too, are worth the electricity.
glossary: retener, negar (algo que se debía dar)

questions.q: The editorial claims that the proposal affects mainly people who have few other places to read or study.
questions.explain_es: Sostiene que los usuarios de la tarde son quienes 'have nowhere else to turn', como la enfermera, el adolescente y el jubilado.

questions.q: The editorial states that the council's argument about limited budgets is entirely false.
questions.explain_es: Reconoce que la tesis del concejo tiene 'some justice' y dice 'We do not dispute this'.

questions.q: What does the writer imply by calling the proposal 'a statement about what the city thinks reading is for'?
options: The city wants to expand its book collection
Reading is seen as a service that can be reduced
The council has never read an official report
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: aunque se presente como 'technicality', recortar horarios muestra que se valora poco la lectura.

questions.q: What is the tone of the question 'How can a city that hosts one of the world's great book fairs justify turning off the lights on its own readers?'
options: Playful and unconcerned about the outcome
Pointedly ironic and critical of a contradiction
Sincerely curious about the council's reasons
questions.explain_es: Tono: es una pregunta retórica que señala la contradicción entre presumir de feria del libro y recortar el acceso a la lectura.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the final paragraph?
options: To announce the closure of the newspaper's office
To summarise the council's budget in detail
To call for withdrawal and state a principle
questions.explain_es: Propósito: exige retirar la propuesta ('We therefore urge the council to withdraw') y cierra con un principio: las ciudades se juzgan por lo que se niegan a recortar.

questions.q: How does the writer deal with the argument about digital access?
options: By refuting it, since a library is more than a store of texts
By ignoring it, since it has no relevance at all
By accepting it, since downloads replace the buildings
questions.explain_es: Estructura argumentativa: refuta la objeción diciendo que 'This confuses a collection with an institution'.

questions.q: In 'a budget is also a moral document', 'moral' suggests that a budget…
options: contains only legal rules
reveals a society's values
depends on private opinions
questions.explain_es: 'Moral document' sugiere que las decisiones presupuestarias muestran qué valores y prioridades tiene una sociedad.

title: The Lost Property Office
topic: Loneliness, objects and small acts of kindness
focus: Free indirect speech and narrative tenses
paragraphs: Tiago had been working the night shift at the lost property office in Lisbon for eight months, and in that time he had come to believe that people lose only what they secretly wish to be rid of. Umbrellas, certainly. Gloves, scarves, a cello once, which no one had ever claimed. But also, in his experience, the letters, the keys to rooms they no longer entered, the wedding ring in a coat pocket. Nobody comes looking for those, he thought, and everybody pretends they were accidents.

The office occupied a basement beneath a station, and its only decoration was a clock that ran four minutes fast. Tiago was paid a little over a thousand euros a month, which in Lisbon felt like a rumour. He took the job to save money for a master's degree in a city where it did not rain so much, and he had told himself that it was temporary. That had been eight months ago, and in the meantime he had become something of a specialist in other people's absences.

One Thursday near closing time, a woman appeared at the counter. She was perhaps seventy, wore a green coat buttoned to the chin and held her handbag in front of her like a shield. She was looking, she said, for a notebook. It was blue, with a rubber band round it. She had left it on the number twenty-eight tram the previous Monday, and she had telephoned three times, and each time a different voice had told her to wait.

Tiago checked the register and then the shelves. There were two notebooks, neither blue, and a diary belonging to a student of dentistry. He apologised. The woman nodded as though she had expected nothing else, and yet she did not leave. She asked, very politely, whether she might sit for a few minutes, because her legs were tired. He found her a chair and a cup of the terrible coffee from the machine, and for a while neither of them spoke.

'It is not valuable,' she said eventually. 'Nobody would steal it. It is just the recipes of my husband, and the things he said while cooking. He did not write well, you understand. He wrote things like add a little more salt, and then sing.' She smiled, and Tiago, who had not been taught how to answer such a sentence, said that he would look again. He said it as one speaks to a child, and was ashamed of it.

That night, when the last train had gone, he searched the entire basement. He opened boxes he had never opened and found a trumpet, a prosthetic hand, two hundred and six single socks. He did not find a blue notebook. At four in the morning he sat down on the floor, amid the abandoned lives of strangers, and did something he had not done since he was a boy: he phoned his own mother, who answered at once, frightened, and then laughed.

The notebook turned up the following week, handed in by a tram driver who had kept it in his cabin because he thought the recipes looked interesting. Tiago telephoned the number the woman had left. When she came for it, she tried to give him a ten-euro note, which he refused, and then she tried to give him a recipe, which he accepted. He still has it. It says: add a little more salt, and then sing. He has noticed that it works rather well on nights when nothing is claimed.

questions.q: The woman asks to sit for a few minutes because her legs are tired.
questions.explain_es: Pide sentarse 'because her legs were tired' y Tiago le busca una silla.

questions.q: The tram driver threw the notebook away because he thought it was worthless.
questions.explain_es: El conductor lo guardó en su cabina 'because he thought the recipes looked interesting'.

questions.q: What can we infer about Tiago's phone call to his mother?
options: He felt isolated and the woman's story affected him
He was angry because she had forgotten his birthday
He wanted to ask her for money to study abroad
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: después de oír a la anciana habla de su marido, llama a su madre 'something he had not done since he was a boy'. El texto sugiere soledad y emoción, no dinero.

questions.q: What is the narrator's tone when describing Tiago's salary as 'a rumour'?
options: Wryly humorous about how little it buys
Admiring of the generosity of the job
Seriously accusatory towards his employers
questions.explain_es: Tono: 'which in Lisbon felt like a rumour' es una ironía suave; sugiere que el sueldo apenas parece real frente al coste de vida.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the opening reflection on what people lose?
options: It introduces the story's theme of absence and care
It describes the woman's coat in detail
It explains how the office is organised
questions.explain_es: Propósito: plantea el tema de lo que se pierde y se abandona; la historia lo matiza con la libreta que sí se reclama.

questions.q: How does the story end?
options: With Tiago leaving the job to study elsewhere
With the recipe becoming a small comfort for Tiago
With the woman complaining to his manager
questions.explain_es: Estructura: el final cierra el círculo con la receta, 'add a little more salt, and then sing', que Tiago conserva y le funciona en noches sin reclamaciones.

questions.q: In 'he had become something of a specialist in other people's absences', 'something of' suggests that Tiago is…
options: officially trained as one
a little like one, in a way
reluctant to become one
questions.explain_es: 'Something of a' atenúa: Tiago es una especie de especialista, no un experto oficial.

title: On Being Wrong Well
paragraphs: Distinguished teachers, proud families, and, above all, fellow graduates: I have been asked to say something wise, which is a little like asking a fish to describe the shore. I am twenty-three years old, I have a degree in economics from the University of Ghana and a fixed-term contract at a small bank in Accra. My credentials for wisdom are therefore limited. What I do have is a record of mistakes, and I propose to spend my ten minutes on them.

Let me begin with the most expensive. In my second year, I wrote an essay arguing, with great confidence, that a particular microcredit scheme was a triumph. My lecturer returned it covered in questions. I was offended, then embarrassed, then, after a long walk and a very bad cup of coffee, curious. The scheme, as it turned out, had worked for some borrowers and ruined others, and my confidence had been built entirely on the first group. I had not been lying; I had merely been looking in one direction.

That is the first lesson I wish to offer: being wrong is rarely a failure of intelligence. It is, far more often, a failure of attention. We see what we expect to see, and we stop looking once we are satisfied. The remedy is not to be cleverer, but to be more patient, and to ask the one question that confident people find hardest to ask: what would I expect to see if I were mistaken?

The second lesson concerns the people around us. Be it a friend, a colleague or a stranger on the internet, the person who corrects you is doing you a favour you will not recognise at the time. I would urge you to thank them, or at least not to punish them. Some of you will become managers, ministers, perhaps even central bankers. Please remember, when you do, that the people who disagree with you are your cheapest source of information.

The third lesson is the most difficult, and I confess that I have not yet mastered it. It is that to be wrong well is to be wrong publicly and without drama. When we err, we are tempted either to defend ourselves until we are ridiculous or to collapse in apology until everyone feels obliged to comfort us. Both are forms of vanity. The better course is a sentence of three parts: I was mistaken; this is what I now believe; this is why.

I know that this advice sounds easy in a hall full of balloons. The world we are entering does not reward it. It rewards certainty, speed and the ability to sound convincing on a very short video. A person who says, I do not know, will often be passed over for the person who says, I am sure. Yet look at how many of the confident have left this country poorer than they found it, and ask yourselves which kind of leadership we have, honestly, been paying for.

So, graduates, I wish you many mistakes, and I wish them early, while they are cheap. I wish you teachers who write questions in the margins, and friends who will tell you when your argument has a hole in it. And on the day you finally discover that you were wrong about something you loved, I wish you the courage to say so aloud, with a steady voice and, if possible, with a little laughter. Thank you, congratulations, and please, someone, check my arithmetic.
glossary: credencial, título o mérito que acredita
pasar por alto, ignorar para un ascenso

questions.q: The speaker's essay about microcredit was based mainly on evidence from borrowers who benefited.
questions.explain_es: Dice que su confianza 'had been built entirely on the first group', es decir, los prestatarios para quienes funcionó.

questions.q: The speaker says that being wrong is usually caused by a lack of intelligence.
questions.explain_es: Afirma que 'being wrong is rarely a failure of intelligence. It is, far more often, a failure of attention'.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the speaker's view of confident leaders?
options: He doubts that confidence alone makes good leadership
He believes that only the confident should lead
He thinks leaders should never speak in public
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: cuestiona si los 'confident' han dejado el país mejor y pregunta qué tipo de liderazgo se ha estado pagando.

questions.q: What is the tone of the closing line 'please, someone, check my arithmetic'?
options: Self-deprecating and warm
Bitter and defensive
Formal and entirely serious
questions.explain_es: Tono: es una broma autocrítica y afectuosa que ilustra la idea central del discurso, aceptar la posibilidad de equivocarse.

questions.q: Why does the speaker begin by calling himself 'a fish describing the shore'?
options: To explain that he used to study marine biology
To criticise the choice of speaker for the day
To admit his limited authority with humour
questions.explain_es: Propósito: usa humor para reconocer que carece de experiencia ('My credentials for wisdom are therefore limited') y ganarse a la audiencia.

questions.q: How does the speech develop its central idea?
options: Through a historical review of banking crises
Through three jokes followed by a long statistic
Through a personal story followed by three lessons
questions.explain_es: Estructura: abre con una anécdota (el ensayo sobre microcrédito), enuncia tres lecciones y cierra con deseos para los graduados.

questions.q: In 'a cup of coffee', the phrase 'a very bad cup of coffee' mainly adds…
options: a precise price detail
a serious complaint about the venue
a touch of ironic humour
questions.explain_es: El detalle del mal café aporta humor irónico y personal, sin queja seria.

title: Firm Introduces Mandatory Spontaneity, Scheduled for Fridays
paragraphs: MADRID. In a bold move that analysts described as both unprecedented and, strictly speaking, contradictory, the management consultancy Vanguardia Partners announced yesterday that all employees will henceforth be required to behave spontaneously between 3.00 and 3.45 every Friday afternoon. Attendance is compulsory, enthusiasm is monitored, and surprise, according to the internal memo, will be 'fully planned and carefully evaluated'.

The initiative, titled Moments of Joy, follows a survey in which forty per cent of staff described the company culture as 'a little grey'. The chief wellbeing officer, Beatriz Montoya, a woman whose business card features a smiling sun, said that management had listened humbly. 'Our people told us they wanted more fun,' she explained. 'We have responded by creating a space in which fun can happen, subject to the availability of the meeting room.'

Under the new policy, employees must register their spontaneous activities forty-eight hours in advance, via a form of eleven pages, to avoid the risk of unplanned laughter. Approved examples include 'a sudden dance', 'an unexpected snack' and 'a surprise compliment to a colleague of equal or lower rank'. Employees wishing to be spontaneous in a more senior direction must first obtain written permission from their line manager and, in some cases, from Legal.

Reactions have been mixed, though the company has asked that they be mixed in a positive proportion. A junior analyst, Mateo Salazar, said he welcomed the change. 'I used to be afraid that my enthusiasm would not be noticed,' he said. 'Now it will be measured, which is much better.' When asked whether he had ever been spontaneous before, he consulted his phone and replied that this was 'outside his current objectives'.

Not everyone is convinced. An employee who asked to remain anonymous, and who was apparently so frightened of the policy that she spoke from inside a cupboard, told our reporter that last Friday's session had begun with a ten-minute presentation about the importance of not presenting. 'Then we were instructed to relax,' she said. 'We were given a diagram. It did not help. I now suffer from a very precise form of anxiety.'

Experts have been cautious. Professor Ignacio Ferrer, who studies organisational behaviour at a Spanish business school, said the policy was 'a fascinating case of an institution attempting to buy something it has spent years destroying'. Asked whether it might work, he paused for several seconds, then added that 'the early data are encouraging, because no one has yet been brave enough to report otherwise'.

The company is already planning a second phase. From next quarter, staff will be invited to take part in Authentic Vulnerability Hour, during which each person will share one genuine fear, approved in advance and limited to ninety seconds. A spokesperson confirmed that the policy would be reviewed after six months, 'unless it is going so well that we cannot bear to review it'. At the time of writing, the company's share price was unchanged, and the cupboard was reportedly occupied.

questions.q: According to the article, employees must register their spontaneous activities in advance.
questions.explain_es: Deben registrarlas 'forty-eight hours in advance, via a form of eleven pages'. La contradicción con la espontaneidad es la base de la sátira.

questions.q: The chief wellbeing officer says that the company ignored the survey results.
questions.explain_es: Ella dice que la dirección 'had listened humbly'. La ironía está en cómo responde, no en que ignore la encuesta.

questions.q: What does the article imply about the company's real attitude to employee freedom?
options: It is indifferent to how workers feel
It wants control even over supposedly free behaviour
It truly trusts workers to be creative
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: se programa y evalúa hasta la sorpresa; la empresa necesita controlarlo todo, incluso lo espontáneo.

questions.q: What is the tone of the article?
options: Deadpan and mockingly absurd
Angry and openly accusatory
Warm and uncritically supportive
questions.explain_es: Tono: imita el estilo de una noticia seria ('deadpan') para ridiculizar la política con detalles absurdos.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the quotation from Professor Ferrer?
options: To give the satire a mock-academic verdict
To provide a serious statistical analysis
To promote his business school
questions.explain_es: Propósito: su frase 'an institution attempting to buy something it has spent years destroying' resume la crítica con apariencia de autoridad; es parte de la parodia.

questions.q: How does the final paragraph develop the satire?
options: It offers a sincere summary of the results
It reports that the policy has been cancelled
It adds an even more absurd second phase
questions.explain_es: Estructura: el cierre intensifica el absurdo con la 'Authentic Vulnerability Hour' limitada a noventa segundos.

questions.q: In 'the cupboard was reportedly occupied', 'reportedly' means…
options: without any doubt at all
according to what people say
after careful official checks
questions.explain_es: 'Reportedly' = según se dice, sin confirmación completa.

title: In Praise of the Unfinished
topic: Incomplete works and the ideal of completion
focus: Cleft sentences and fronting for emphasis
paragraphs: Every writer I know keeps a drawer. In mine, there are two novels abandoned at page sixty, a half-translated play and a letter to a former teacher that I began in 2019 and never sent. For years I regarded this drawer as a small, private graveyard. Lately I have started to see it differently: not as a record of failure but as a map of everything I once considered worth attempting, which is perhaps a better definition of a life.

Our culture is not kind to unfinished things. We admire completion, the launched product, the signed contract, the final chapter, and we measure people by what they have delivered. Yet some of the most moving works we know were never completed. Schubert's Symphony in B minor, known to the world as the Unfinished, survives in two movements, and no audience has ever left a concert hall feeling cheated. Nor does it seem to matter that Barcelona's Sagrada Família, begun in 1882, is still under construction.

What I find interesting is not that these works are incomplete, but that we agree to love them anyway. It is the sense of an interrupted intention that attracts us, the feeling of arriving in the middle of someone's thought. A finished work says: here is what I decided. An unfinished one says: here is what I was trying to decide, and it invites us, almost against our will, to continue the conversation.

There is, of course, a cheaper version of this argument, and I wish to distance myself from it. Laziness is not a philosophy, and the fact that a masterpiece may be unfinished does not make every abandoned draft a masterpiece. Most of what lives in my drawer is there because it was not good enough, or because I was afraid. To pretend otherwise would be vanity of a particularly flattering kind: the kind that disguises avoidance as depth.

Still, there is a real difference between work abandoned in fear and work set aside in good conscience. It is the second that deserves respect. A translator who stops because she realises she has misunderstood the original, a painter who leaves a canvas because the next stroke would spoil it, an architect who builds only the foundation of a house because the funds have run out and the family cannot wait: each has made a judgement, and judgements are always provisional.

Perhaps what we really fear in the unfinished is not the absence of an ending but the presence of time. A completed object seems to defy it; an incomplete one reminds us that we, too, are works under construction, with scaffolding still visible. Those who are comfortable with that reminder tend to be gentler with themselves and, curiously, more productive, since they no longer need each project to prove that they are finished people.

So I intend to keep my drawer. I shall add to it, with luck, and I may even return to the letter, whose first line I still like. Whether I finish it or not matters less than I once believed. What matters is that the intention was real, and that it remains, quietly, on the page: a small unfinished sentence, waiting for someone, perhaps myself, to find the next word.

questions.q: The author believes that every abandoned draft is secretly a masterpiece.
questions.explain_es: Lo rechaza: 'the fact that a masterpiece may be unfinished does not make every abandoned draft a masterpiece' y admite que muchos borradores están ahí por miedo.

questions.q: The author mentions that Schubert's Unfinished Symphony has two movements.
questions.explain_es: El texto dice que 'survives in two movements'.

questions.q: What does the author imply about her own drawer of unfinished work?
options: It contains works she once thought worth trying
It should be burned to avoid embarrassment
It proves that she lacks all creative talent
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: lo ve como 'a map of everything I once considered worth attempting', no como fracaso puro.

questions.q: What is the author's attitude to the 'cheaper version' of the argument?
options: Delighted, since it excuses her habits
Indifferent, since it is irrelevant
Wary, since it excuses laziness
questions.explain_es: Actitud: se distancia ('I wish to distance myself') porque 'Laziness is not a philosophy'.

questions.q: Why does the author mention the translator, the painter and the architect?
options: To illustrate good-faith reasons for stopping
To argue that artists should never start works
To list jobs that always end without success
questions.explain_es: Propósito: son ejemplos de obras dejadas por una decisión razonable ('each has made a judgement').

questions.q: How does the essay close?
options: By quoting a long passage from Schubert
By returning to the opening image of the drawer
By introducing a completely new argument
questions.explain_es: Estructura: se vuelve al cajón del comienzo ('I intend to keep my drawer'), con una estructura circular.

questions.q: In 'a translator who stops because she realises she has misunderstood', 'misunderstood' shows that she…
options: read the original wrongly
wrote the draft too quickly
disliked the original author
questions.explain_es: 'Misunderstood' = entender mal; ella interpretó el original de forma incorrecta.

title: Why Rivers Wander
paragraphs: Few things in nature appear as casual as a river in a flat landscape. It slides across the plain in long, lazy loops, doubling back on itself as if undecided about the sea. The impression of indecision is, however, misleading. A meandering river is not wandering at random; it is following the physics of moving water, and the shape it adopts is one of the most reliable patterns in the earth sciences. The word itself comes from the Maeander, an ancient name for a famously winding river in what is now Turkey.

The explanation begins with a small irregularity. No river is perfectly straight, and wherever the channel bends slightly, the water behaves differently on the two sides. On the outer edge of the bend, the current is faster and the water cuts into the bank, removing soil and sand. On the inner edge, the flow slows, and the sediment it was carrying is dropped. Over years, the outside bank retreats while the inside grows, forming a curved deposit often called a point bar.

The consequence is that the bend becomes sharper. A sharper curve accentuates the difference between the two sides, and the process feeds itself. Meanders are therefore not static but migratory: the whole loop slowly drifts downstream and sideways across the floodplain. On a map made fifty years ago, a river may sit in a noticeably different place from the one it occupies today, which can be a serious problem for those who farm, build or draw national borders along it.

Eventually, a meander may grow so exaggerated that its neck, the narrow strip of land between two parts of the loop, is almost cut through. During a flood, the river may take the shortcut. The old loop is abandoned, its ends sealed with sediment, and it remains as a curved, isolated body of water known as an oxbow lake. These crescent-shaped lakes can be seen in many floodplains, from the lower Mississippi to the lowlands of South America, and they are rich in wildlife.

It is tempting to treat such behaviour as a nuisance, and engineers have often done so. Rivers have been straightened, embanked and held in concrete channels in the hope of making them predictable. The results have been mixed. A straightened river flows faster, carries more energy downstream and can worsen flooding in towns lower down. Some of the most costly engineering projects of the last century are now being quietly reversed, with channels returned to their loops.

Researchers also point out that meandering is not a purely terrestrial habit. Similar patterns have been observed in meltwater channels on glaciers, in ocean currents and, in radar images, in channels on other worlds. The geometry of a bend, it seems, is a general solution to a general problem: how a fluid on a gentle slope disposes of its energy. The river, in this sense, is not wandering. It is calculating, slowly and in public.

The lesson for the rest of us is perhaps a modest one. What appears to be disorder is often the visible result of a rule, and what looks like a detour may turn out to be the shortest route available. A river that has been allowed to wander usually knows more about its valley than any map. Those who have lived beside one for generations, and who have learned to watch where the bank is falling, have long suspected as much.

questions.q: Water flows faster on the outer edge of a river bend than on the inner edge.
questions.explain_es: Dice que 'On the outer edge of the bend, the current is faster', mientras que en el interior el flujo es lento y se deposita sedimento.

questions.q: The article says that straightening a river always reduces flooding.
questions.explain_es: Lo contrario: un río enderezado 'flows faster' y 'can worsen flooding in towns lower down'.

questions.q: What can be inferred about maps drawn fifty years ago?
options: They were drawn without knowing river physics
They always show the same river course today
They may show a river in a different position
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: los meandros migran, así que un mapa antiguo puede situar el río en otro lugar ('may sit in a noticeably different place').

questions.q: What is the tone of the final sentence about people who live beside rivers?
options: Mocking of traditional beliefs
Critical of their lack of education
Respectful of local, long-term knowledge
questions.explain_es: Tono: reconoce que quienes viven junto al río 'have long suspected as much', valorando su saber acumulado.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the mention of meltwater channels and other worlds?
options: To prove that all rivers originate on glaciers
To show that meandering is a general fluid pattern
To suggest that engineers copy these patterns exactly
questions.explain_es: Propósito: ilustra que el meandro es 'a general solution to a general problem', no algo exclusivo de los ríos terrestres.

questions.q: How does the article develop its explanation?
options: From a legend to a set of engineering rules
From a puzzling appearance to a cause, consequences and implications
From an interview to a list of famous rivers
questions.explain_es: Estructura: parte de la apariencia de indecisión, explica la causa física, las consecuencias (migración, lagos) y la lección general.

questions.q: In 'a nuisance', as in 'treat such behaviour as a nuisance', the writer suggests the behaviour is seen as…
options: an annoying problem
a legal duty
a rare marvel
questions.explain_es: 'Nuisance' es una molestia; los ingenieros han visto el comportamiento del río como un problema a controlar.
